directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool and pruning to an open vase shape each winter for easier harvest among the thorns. Hinnonmaki Yellow is the golden-fruited counterpart to the widely grown Hinnonmaki Red, bred in Finland from the same mildew-tolerant lineage and sharing its compact, upright, spiny habit. The translucent amber berries ripen a little later than the red form and carry a milder, honeyed sweetness many gardeners prefer straight off the bush, while both hold up well cooked into pies and preserves. Best suited to cool-summer climates, since heat and humidity bring on powdery mildew and fruit stress.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into fertile, well-manured soil; prune to an open framework since heavily laden branches tend to arch under the crop's weight.

directions: Plant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into fertile, well-manured soil, since Leveller needs steady moisture to size its fruit. This Victorian-era English dessert gooseberry, first raised in the 1850s, is still grown for its very large, pale yellow-green, thin-skinned berries with an exceptionally rich, sweet flavor once fully ripe. It is a vigorous, somewhat spreading bush that is more prone to American gooseberry mildew than modern disease-resistant releases, so good airflow matters in humid climates. Best reserved for dedicated fruit growers in cool-summer regions willing to manage its mildew susceptibility for the sake of exceptional flavor.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

Achilles is a mildew-resistant red gooseberry developed at England's East Malling Research Station, valued for pairing heavy, reliable cropping with much better resistance to American gooseberry mildew than older varieties like Leveller. The medium-large, smooth berries ripen to a deep pinkish-red with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor good for both fresh eating and cooking. Its upright, moderately vigorous bush is easier to manage and pick than sprawling heirloom types, making it a practical choice for smaller home orchards.

directions: Plant dormant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Oregon Champion is a nineteenth-century American heirloom gooseberry long favored in the Pacific Northwest for combining decent mildew tolerance with the classic tartness of European-type gooseberries. The medium-sized, pale yellow-green berries have a smooth, faintly fuzzy skin and hold their tang well, making them as useful for pies and preserves as for fresh eating once fully ripe. The vigorous, spiny bush handles the region's cool, damp summers better than many English exhibition varieties.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood-cutting-propagated bushes in fall into fertile soil in full sun to light shade; remove the oldest third of stems each winter to keep productive new wood coming.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall into fertile soil in full sun to light shade, removing the oldest third of stems each winter to keep productive new wood coming. White Imperial is a long-cultivated heirloom white currant prized as one of the sweetest and mildest of all currant varieties, with translucent, creamy-white berries pleasant enough to eat straight off the strig rather than only cooked into preserves. The upright, productive bush ripens long clusters in midsummer and is self-fertile, so a single bush sets a full crop. Its mild flavor and pale, attractive fruit make it popular for fresh eating, garnishing, and pale jellies where a less tart currant is wanted.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide
